title: Variance: The Shortcut and the Rules
short: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X).
trouble: Students write Var(aX + b) = a Var(X) + b, which makes Var(−X) negative.

blocks.html: The standard deviation of a random variable measures how far $X$ typically lands from its mean. Its square, the variance, is easier to work with, because it is an expected value of a function: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^{2}]$ with $\mu = E[X]$.

Shortcut: expand $(X - \mu)^{2} = X^{2} - 2\mu X + \mu^{2}$ and use linearity: $E[X^{2}] - 2\mu \cdot \mu + \mu^{2} = E[X^{2}] - \mu^{2}$.
Linear change: $aX + b$ has mean $a\mu + b$, so its distance from its mean is $(aX + b) - (a\mu + b) = a(X - \mu)$. Squaring gives $a^{2}(X - \mu)^{2}$, and averaging gives $a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)$. The shift $b$ moves every value and the mean together, so it disappears.

blocks.title: A die
blocks.q: Find the variance and standard deviation of a fair die roll.

blocks.title: A linear change
blocks.q: $X$ is a fair die roll and $Y = 3 - 2X$. Find $E[Y]$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ and $\operatorname{SD}(Y)$.

blocks.html: Two more facts come straight from the shortcut. Rearranged, it says $E[X^{2}] = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \mu^{2}$. More generally, for any number $c$, $$E[(X - c)^{2}] = \operatorname{Var}(X) + (\mu - c)^{2},$$ because $X - c = (X - \mu) + (\mu - c)$ and the cross term has mean $2(\mu - c)E[X - \mu] = 0$. So the average squared distance from $c$ is smallest when $c = \mu$: the mean is the best single guess when errors are measured by their squares.

blocks.title: Changing units
blocks.q: Daily highs have mean $20^\circ\text{C}$ and standard deviation $5^\circ\text{C}$. Find the mean and standard deviation in Fahrenheit, $F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$.
steps: Standard deviation: $\frac{9}{5} \cdot 5 = 9^\circ\text{F}$; adding 32 does not change the spread.

blocks.title: Squared distance from a target
blocks.q: $X$ has mean 5 and variance 4. Find $E[X^{2}]$ and $E[(X - 2)^{2}]$.

blocks.html: Variance is measured in squared units (square degrees, square dollars), which is hard to picture. The standard deviation, its square root, is back in the original units, so use the SD when describing spread and the variance when calculating.

Writing $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a\operatorname{Var}(X) + b$. With $a = -1$ and $b = 0$ that would make $\operatorname{Var}(-X)$ negative, which is impossible; and adding a constant cannot change how spread out the values are. Check: a variance is never negative, and $\operatorname{Var}(-X) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$.
